newsitem.title: CHINA: China says 10 foreign banks want to do yuan trade.
newsitem.headline: China says 10 foreign banks want to do yuan trade.

text.p: A total of 10 foreign financial institutions are on a waiting list to be the first to win permission to handle business in China's domestic yuan currency by the end of the year, the Xinhua news agency said on Tuesday.
"Our bank is now working actively to draft specific rules for foreign banks to follow," Xinhua quoted an official of the Shanghai office of the People's Bank of China, the central bank, as saying.
The rules would follow regulations issued last week by the central bank governing management of trial business in the yuan, he said.

The rules will govern the reserve ratio that foreign banks must keep with the central bank's local branch, how the banks should join the national interbank money market and abide by local rules on money management and accounting, he said. He gave no details.
"We have been redoubling efforts with the preparation work to help qualified foreign banks win central bank approval," he said, adding that the deadline for first approvals was the end of this year.
Foreign banks are now restricted to business in foreign currency and have been eager to gain a share of the business for taking deposits and making loans in yuan.
The official said 10 banks were on the waiting list but did not identify them.

The official Shanghai Star newspaper has already said three banks -- Citicorp's Citibank unit, Tokyo-Mitsubishi Bank and HSBC Corp's Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp -- would be given licences for local currency business.
The policy relaxation would apply only to banks in Shanghai's Pudong district, an area that China's economic planners have been eager to promote, the official said.
Regulations unveiled last week said chosen foreign banks would not be allowed to have local currency debts exceeding 35 percent of their foreign currency debts.
Commercial bankers said that appeared to mean that China would restrict the amount of business by placing a limit on the deposits a foreign bank could accept.
